articles.full_text:
AI Report Anthropic Five weird details from Anthropic’s IPO filing From conscious AI and ‘catastrophic’ risk to unusual corporate structures and executive perks.

From conscious AI and ‘catastrophic’ risk to unusual corporate structures and executive perks. by Robert Hart Oct 26, 2026, 5:10 PM UTC Link Share Gift Image: The Verge Robert Hart is a London-based reporter at The Verge covering all things AI and a Senior Tarbell Fellow.

Previously, he wrote about health, science and tech for Forbes .

Anthropic has finally filed its S-1 prospectus with the SEC, a document designed to give investors a look under the hood of its business, from how much its executives are making and plans for spending its IPO billions to the risks that could derail its ambitions.

At more than 300 pages, there’s a lot to unpack, and some of the disclosures have not previously been reported.

Here are some of the biggest things that jumped out to us from our first pass: It pays to be an Amodei Sibling co-founders Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei are the two most highly-paid executives at Anthropic, according to the filing.

Last year, CEO Dario’s compensation totaled nearly $18 million, most of which came from stock and option awards.

President Daniela, meanwhile, received $16.4 million.

Admittedly, it is at the lower end of the Big Tech scale , but it is still a tidy sum.

And that’s not all.

Anthropic also spent $2.75 million on “personal security services” for Dario and $1.29 million for “personal protection, home security, and transportation services” for Daniela.

Dario also gets access to a private jet for personal use, which cost the company another $97,055.

The company says its success is “highly dependent on the continued service” of its senior team, particularly Dario and Daniela, who “are critical” to advancing the company’s research and mission.

Anthropic has some pretty existential risk factors Every S-1 features a long list of things that could go wrong.

Anthropic’s is no exception.

But alongside standard warnings about competition, regulation, and market shifts, there are some less conventional risks too.

For one, Anthropic warns that AI systems could cause potentially “catastrophic” harm, potentially of a kind that could not be underwritten by the entire “insurance industry in the aggregate.” As AI systems become more sophisticated, there’s also the question of whether Claude — or any other AI system — could possess or develop “forms of sentience.” Such a scenario would present some rather unusual business challenges.

There’s also the possibility they “may behave in unintended, misaligned, or autonomous ways” that could damage the company.

It’s hungry for compute It’s no secret that Anthropic needs compute, but the sheer scale of its spending is staggering.

The filing details billions of dollars of commitments to secure the compute needed to power its AI models, including roughly $3.1 billion per month to SpaceX for access to Nvidia GPUs once all of the planned capacity is delivered, totaling as much as $120.5 billion by 2029.

Other commitments include spending $44.9 billion with Microsoft through 2033, at least $114.5 billion with Google through 2033, and $110 billion with Amazon over the next ten years.

Anthropic also plans to expand its own “infrastructure footprint,” including overseas, as it faces increasing opposition to data center development in the US.

It has a really weird corporate structure Anthropic already has a somewhat complicated corporate structure as a public benefit corporation.

But there’s another unusual twist that will allow its seven cofounders to retain considerable control over the company even after it goes public.

Through a separate corporate entity called “Founder LLC,” the group will collectively control 50.1 percent of shareholder voting power over key matters.

Anthropic says the seven founders “are distinctly equipped to be stewards of our mission” of benefiting humanity through responsible AI development.

Anthropic names only two rivals There’s no shortage of AI models out there, but when it comes to “direct competition,” Anthropic names just two other developers: OpenAI and Google.

Condolences to SpaceX, Meta, and the rest of the AI world.

articles.title: Anthropic’s IPO filing reveals its strategy for keeping enterprise customers hooked
articles.reason: 涵盖 AI product & news、Startup & business
articles.summary: Anthropic’s S-1 shows more than half of its $100,000-plus customers now use both the Claude Platform and a first-party app, a cross-selling playbook reminiscent of Amazon that’s making enterprise customers stickier.
articles.full_text:
Anthropic is building the same kind of cross-product ecosystem that helped make tech companies like Amazon and Uber enormously sticky, and its S-1 suggests the strategy is working.

More than half of customers spending at least $100,000 annually now use both the Claude platform and a first-party app like Claude Code or Cowork, up from about 30% at the end of last year. “The speed and depth of our enterprise customer adoption are powerful evidence of Claude’s position at the frontier of AI,” the S-1, filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday , reads.

As of September 30, Anthropic recorded more than 11,900 customers spending at least $100,000; more than 1,900 customers spending upward of $1 million; and about 250 customers spending $10 million or more annually.

Anthropic attributes customer momentum to a “significant usage expansion as customers realize the value of deploying Claude across their organizations,” which drove net revenue retention of about 900% as of the end of the third quarter.  Throwing shade at the entire legacy SaaS industry, Anthropic pitches Claude as not a “static product that serves a single use case,” but rather “frontier AI with rapidly advancing capabilities” spanning the models, the developer platform, and the applications users interact with directly.  “An advance at any layer compounds across all three layers, accelerating the pace at which we can deliver more capable intelligence,” the filing reads, calling this “integrated approach” the reason more customers use both the Claude Platform and first-party apps.

The playbook is familiar.

Uber began by selling rides but has expanded into food delivery and freight.

With AWS, Amazon drew in customers with cloud computing services before expanding those relationships into storage, databases, and other offerings, making the ecosystem increasingly hard to leave.

Like those companies, Anthropic doesn’t have to sell each product to a brand-new buyer: A business that starts with the API can deploy Claude Code to their engineers and then Cowork to their broader workforce.

Those app users become far more valuable.

In the third quarter, the highest-spending 5% of Claude Enterprise customers who used Claude Code spent about 20x as much per month as the average enterprise user who didn’t use the coding tool, per the filing.

The finding demonstrates how much room there is for per-user spend to grow, and illustrates why Anthropic is keen to get its applications into the accounts that start with the API.

Anthropic said it amplifies that organic diffusion by investing in Applied AI teams.

An internal Applied AI team works with startups and enterprises to help place Claude inside customers’ existing technology stacks, and the company recently launched a separate venture with Blackstone and other private equity firms, dubbed Ode with Anthropic, to embed forward-deployed engineers into businesses to build bespoke AI tools with Claude.

Anthropic also leans on its third-party distribution partnerships with hyperscalers AWS, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure.

Under what the filing calls a “joint go-to-market approach,” Anthropic holds the direct contractual relationship with customers and pays each cloud provider a fee, which the company says lets it “avoid channel conflict” and “set pricing.” Anthropic’s budding stickiness strategy may become essential as the AI giant seeks to constantly “reinvent our business” by releasing “new classes of products whose aim is to dwarf the economic value of our existing ones.” The company says it will devote less effort than a typical business to “entrenching our current products and business models, and more effort to defining new ones.” The filing also flags headwinds, despite impressive revenue growth of $16.3 billion for the first half of 2026, up from $1.2 billion in the same period last year.

The cloud partnerships that help sell Claude are increasingly seeing Anthropic as a competitor, which Anthropic says could lead to difficulties securing the compute it needs from them.

The filing states that Amazon, Google, and Microsoft may prioritize their own requirements or rivals they’ve invested in.

Customer concentration is another risk.  “Any adverse change in demand from our largest customers … could adversely affect our business and prospects,” reads part of the risk factors section. “As a result, a significant reduction in spending by, or the loss of, one or more of our largest customers, if not offset by new customer relationships or increased business from our other existing customers, could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.” Anthropic did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment.

articles.title: Anthropic officially files for its public debut
articles.reason: 涵盖 AI product & news、Startup & business
articles.summary: Anthropic has officially filed for an IPO, revealing soaring revenue, mounting losses, major enterprise adoption, and an unusual governance structure designed to preserve founder control and its AI safety mission.
articles.full_text:
After weeks of leaked S-1s , Anthropic finally filed for an initial public offering on Monday, setting the stage for one of the most closely watched public debuts in modern U.S. history.

Anthropic, which plans to list under the ticker “ANT,” recorded revenue of $16.3 billion for the first half of 2026, up from $1.2 billion in the same period last year, according to the firm’s latest SEC filing.

That revenue came off the back of an operating loss of $693 million, an improvement from the $2.1 billion in operating losses that Anthropic recorded in the first half of 2025.

Anthropic’s net loss, however, hit $80.7 billion, which was largely driven by noncash accounting adjustments tied to convertible debt. The company says it “may not achieve or sustain profitability in the future.” The filing also provided more color on the scale of Anthropic’s enterprise business.

As of the end of September, Anthropic had more than 11,900 customers spending $100,000 or more annually; 1,900 customers spending $1 million or more; and about 250 customers spending $10 million or more.  As previously reported , Anthropic’s governance structure will enable Anthropic’s seven co-founders to maintain control once the company goes public.

Dario Amodei, Daniela Amodei, Tom Brown, Jack Clark, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish, and Christopher Olah will make up the “Founder LLC,” which will collectively control 50.1% of shareholder voting power — a move Anthropic says is designed to preserve the company’s AI safety mission, per the filing.

Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust, established in 2023 to ensure the company pursues its public benefit mission , will have the authority to appoint most of the company’s board.  The governance structure is controversial because it means voting power is not proportional to the founders’ economic ownership, and therefore public shareholders will have little practical control over a company building technology that, by its own admission, poses “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.” Anthropic hasn’t yet disclosed how much it hopes to raise nor its proposed share price.

AI Business News Anthropic’s IPO filing lays out a plan to ‘revolutionize every area of human endeavor’ with AI The company said it plans to list on the Nasdaq exchange under the ticker ‘ANT.’ The company said it plans to list on the Nasdaq exchange under the ticker ‘ANT.’ by Robert Hart Oct 26, 2026, 1:32 PM UTC Link Share Gift Image: The Verge Robert Hart is a London-based reporter at The Verge covering all things AI and a Senior Tarbell Fellow.

Previously, he wrote about health, science and tech for Forbes .

Anthropic has filed its S-1 prospectus with the Securities and Exchange Commission, preparing the company behind Claude to beat OpenAI to the punch with an IPO.

In a filing with the SEC, Anthropic said it plans to list on the Nasdaq exchange under the ticker symbol “ANT.” The AI company confidentially filed with the SEC earlier this year in June, but the public document reveals more details, as well as the company’s plans for the future in its own words, as well as potential risks for investors and the world.

According to the S-1, in the first half of this year Anthropic had an $80.7 billion net loss on $16.3 billion in revenue.

As previously reported by the Wall Street Journal based on leaked versions of the document, the majority of that loss is from accounting charges related to notes issued by the company for funding.

Related Five weird details from Anthropic’s IPO filing It also lays out billions of dollars in deals it’s made for access to compute to power its AI, including about $3.1 billion per month to SpaceX for access to Nvidia GPUs once all of the planned capacity is delivered, totaling as much as $120.5 billion by 2029.

Other commitments include spending $44.9 billion with Microsoft through 2033, at least $114.5 billion with Google through 2033, and $110 billion with Amazon over the next ten years.

Anthropic: We believe that AI is one of the most consequential technologies in human history.

If managed well, it could rapidly accelerate scientific innovation, greatly increase economic growth rates, bring cures for major diseases within reach, and solve problems that have resisted generations of human effort.

Anthropic aims to realize these benefits while navigating and preventing the risks that come with a technological revolution this fast and this powerful.

There are four things that we would like any investor in Anthropic to understand: the incredible potential of AI, the risks we must address, Anthropic’s unique approach to building a company and operating in the world, and the ways in which our behavior may differ from that of a purely profit-maximizing company.

According to the filing, cofounder and chief executive officer Dario Amodei’s compensation totaled nearly $18 million in 2025, most of which came from stock and option awards.

His sister, Daniela Amodei, who also cofounded the company and serves as its president and director, was the second highest-paid executive, receiving $16.4 million in 2025.

Anthropic set out a long list of risk factors that could affect its business, including the prospect of its AI models developing “forms of sentience,” “AI-specific taxes,” and unfavorable resolutions to the many ongoing copyright disputes relating to how its models are trained.

The company also warned about the risk of “catastrophic” AI-related incidents, and said it was likely no single insurer — “and potentially the insurance industry in the aggregate” — could underwrite such risk.
